newsitem.title: CHILE: Clouds mar Chile's sunny economic horizon.
newsitem.headline: Clouds mar Chile's sunny economic horizon.

text.p: On paper, Chile's robust economy looks like a textbook model -- steady growth, low inflation, sensible investment rules.

In fact, the economy is doing so well that Chileans confidently predict their country will join the ranks of the developed world in as little as 15 years, with income and living standards comparable to those of southern Europe.
But amid this promising outlook, a few analysts are looking more closely at the pitfalls of Chile's prosperity -- in particular, an economy bound to a single commodity and a widening income gap.
Chile's spectacular growth has been concentrated in only a few sectors, particularly copper mining, and a long-awaited diversification of exports by and large has not happened.
Development has come almost entirely on the basis of wholesale exploitation of natural resources, with a worsening in environmental ills and benefits varying drastically across the country.
"You look closely at the Chilean economy and you see a picture of a Saudi-type economy. But instead of oil, it's copper," said David Gallagher, a prominent financial consultant in Santiago.

"The mentality is that you can get by by exploiting natural resources and that for anything brain-intensive, you imitate," he said. "And that translates into serious weakness for the Chilean economy and its future prospects."

Gallagher sees a clear parallel between Chile's current dependence on copper and its exploitation early in this century of nitrates, which were used to make explosives. The bottom fell out of nitrates in the 1920s when synthetic explosives were invented.

Barely a month goes by without an announcement of a huge new copper project or an expansion at an existing mine. This year the Australian-owned Escondida mine surpassed state-owned Chuquicamata to become the world's largest copper mine.
At least four more copper megaprojects, three of them foreign-owned, are coming on stream or are on the drawing board.

They are expected to raise copper's share of total Chilean exports from about 40 percent now to more than 50 percent at the end of the century -- down from about 80 percent in the early 1970s, but still a worrying trend.
"Chile is putting a lot of eggs in one basket," said a foreign bank manager in Santiago. "The only people really making money here are in copper and construction."

Despite Chile's reputation for a sleek, modern economy, copper still plays much the same role it did a century ago. The budget is written on the basis of copper prices, exchange rates are heavily influenced by them, and newspapers publish them every day.

Chile is only now starting to bring its decrepit road network and infrastructure up to speed, and development has been sharply skewed along regional lines, benefiting certain parts of the country more than others.
Santiago, centre of Chile's vigorous consumer culture and service economy, and the copper-rich north are both thriving while much of the south has lagged, various reports show.

A recent report by the Santiago office of the U.N. Development Programme said export-oriented regions were progressing far more quickly than others, urban areas over rural, and Santiago over the rest of the country.

"It's not normal for a country of Chile's development level to have such a great gap between the rich and the poor. It's not a gap you find in the developed world nor in most of the poorer countries," said Senator Carlos Ominami, a former economy minister.

Chile had about 1.6 million fewer people living in poverty last year than in 1987 thanks to the economy's growth. But wealthier strata benefited far more from growth due to regressive tax codes and low social spending on education and job training, said the report.
President Eduardo Frei has stressed eliminating extreme poverty and improving education as key campaigns of his government.
However, both drives so far have been "more talk than action," said Gallagher, but even Frei has said Chileans will need generations of effort to pull themselves out of poverty.
Some analysts see a real and frightening possibility of a country in 20 years with a booming economy atop a sea of unskilled, underpaid citizens.

"We are producing social segregation, not just for this year, but for the next 20 years. It's brutal," Socialist Senator Jaime Gazmuri said in the Santiago newspaper El Mercurio. "And in that respect, the country has gone backwards. It has not modernised."
